A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the performance of matrix factorization techniques is not sensitive to the dimension of the vectors in the training collection, as long as the number of samples is sufficiently large.
the sample complexity of matrix factorization techniques is not worse than for the case when one has access to the exact matrix to factorize.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sample complexity of matrix factorizations is not necessarily related to the dimension of the data, but rather to the rank and number of factors of the considered matrix.
, for a given matrix factorization technique, the quality of the factors can be controlled by the number of training examples.
, for the considered matrix decomposition techniques, the empirical average can be used as a proxy of the true expected cost, provided that the number of training samples is large enough.
